units.translation: And the men of the ships are conspicuous to see, with dark limbs amid white robes.
And seven lordly chiefs, conspicuous in the army's spear-shaking array, take their stand at the seventh gate.
A gathering of women advances, conspicuous in dark cloaks.
Her cheek is conspicuous, bloodied with gashes.
My sister, conspicuous in mournful grief.
Conspicuous in form, like a bull that destroys cattle.
πρέψαι: to make like; Aeschylus (fr. 405).
Alas for mortal affairs! When prosperous, one might compare them to a shadow.
I think an unmixed cry is fitting in the city.
A vapor like that from a tomb is fitting.
But greet him well; for indeed it is fitting.
It is not fitting to weep or lament.
It is not fitting to defile a day of good omen with a tongue that brings bad news.
It is fitting to sing a paean.
It is fitting to yield with unbending resolve.
It is not fitting to approach this house.
It is fitting for a woman to praise with her spear before the man who has appeared.
For the prosperous, even defeat is fitting.
As is fitting for newcomers.
Fitting beginnings of life.
For it is not fitting for inferiors to speak boldly.
It is fitting for a herald to report each thing clearly.
It is fitting for the mixed-cry dithyramb to accompany.

Thus I corrected what is written in M as πρεσβήμολοι [envoy-come], changed by others to πρέσβυς μόλοι [old man, come]. The forms πρέσβεως [of an envoy], πρέσβεις [envoys], πρέσβεων [of envoys], πρέσβεσι [to envoys] are frequent, but the nominative πρέσβις [envoy], of which examples are rare, has scarcely anywhere been left untouched by scribes, about which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1585.
For perhaps either a herald or an envoy may come.
